title: Like, Would Like and Past Wishes
summary: Use -ing and to-infinitives after like, love and hate, recognising the difference between enjoyment and a preferred way of acting. Express present wishes with would like or would love, use -ing after mind and enjoy, and describe missed opportunities with would like to have + past participle.
learningObjectives: Use -ing or to-infinitive after like, love and hate for general repeated activities.
Use -ing for enjoyment of an existing situation and distinguish enjoyment from a preferred practice.
Express a specific wish with would like, would love or would prefer + to-infinitive and requests with would mind + -ing.
Express feelings about missed past opportunities using would like/love/prefer to have + past participle.

explanation.heading: Like, love and hate with general activities
explanation.body: For habits and repeated activities, like, love and hate can often take either -ing or a to-infinitive. In many everyday statements, both forms are acceptable. Use the context to decide whether the speaker is talking about an ongoing experience or a preferred practice.
explanation.example: My cousins love visiting small towns at weekends.

explanation.heading: Existing experiences usually take -ing
explanation.body: When the activity or situation is already a reality and the speaker is judging that experience, -ing is generally the natural choice. If someone already lives in a city and enjoys it, say they like living there. This does not describe a future plan.
explanation.example: Nadia enjoys studying in the quiet room she uses every day.

explanation.heading: Enjoyment versus a chosen habit
explanation.body: Like doing commonly means taking pleasure in the activity. Like to do may instead mean choosing or preferring a practice, even when the action itself is not enjoyable. These meanings overlap in some contexts, so do not assume that to always implies dislike.
explanation.example: I do not enjoy tidying, but I like to clear my desk before leaving work.

explanation.heading: Would like and would mind
explanation.body: Would like, would love, would hate and would prefer normally take a to-infinitive to express wishes or preferences, often about a particular occasion. Contrast this with general likes. To make a polite request, would you mind is followed by -ing. Enjoy and mind also take -ing, not a to-infinitive.
explanation.example: I would love to join the tour tomorrow. Would you mind sending me the details?

explanation.heading: Looking back at a missed opportunity
explanation.body: Would like/love/hate/prefer + to have + past participle looks back at something that did not happen or was not possible. It expresses a present reaction to an imagined past experience. The perfect infinitive points backwards in time; would like to do normally concerns a present or future possibility.
explanation.example: I would like to have heard the discussion, but I arrived after it ended.

left.label: Enjoy the activity
left.example: I like cooking with my friends.
left.note: The speaker takes pleasure in cooking.

right.label: Prefer a routine
right.example: I like to prepare ingredients before guests arrive.
right.note: The speaker prefers this practical habit; enjoyment is not the focus.

comparisons.title: General liking versus a specific wish

left.label: General preference
left.note: This is a broad preference or repeated enjoyment.

right.label: Specific intention
right.example: Ella would like to visit the new gallery on Sunday.
right.note: Would like to visit describes a particular wish.

examples.sentence: Since moving to the coast, Hugo has loved living close to the sea.
examples.note: Loved living evaluates an existing experience.

examples.sentence: I like to back up my documents before making a large change.
examples.note: Like to back up describes a chosen protective routine.

examples.sentence: We would like to reserve a table for this evening.
examples.note: Would like to reserve expresses a wish on a particular occasion.

examples.sentence: Would you mind waiting outside for a moment?
examples.note: Would mind takes -ing to make a polite request.

examples.sentence: I would love to have watched the match in person, but I was working.
examples.note: Would love to have watched refers to an unrealised past opportunity.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I enjoy to read on the train.
commonMistakes.correct: I enjoy reading on the train.
commonMistakes.why: Enjoy takes an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I would like visiting the museum tomorrow.
commonMistakes.correct: I would like to visit the museum tomorrow.
commonMistakes.why: Would like followed by an action normally takes a to-infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Would you mind to open the window?
commonMistakes.correct: Would you mind opening the window?
commonMistakes.why: Would you mind + -ing is the normal polite-request pattern.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I would love to have see the concert last week.
commonMistakes.correct: I would love to have seen the concert last week.
commonMistakes.why: The perfect infinitive requires have + past participle: have seen.

studyTips: Describe an activity you already do and enjoy with -ing; describe a routine you choose to follow with like to + verb.
Compare two statements about the same action: I like visiting the park versus I would like to visit the park tomorrow.
To describe a missed opportunity, practise the structure would like to have + past participle with a clear past-time clue.

exercises.prompt: Zara has worked at the community café for two years and enjoys it. She likes ___ there.
exercises.feedback: Because Zara is describing enjoyment of her existing job, likes working is natural.

exercises.prompt: I do not enjoy this chore, but I ___ the dishes straight after dinner so the sink stays clear.
exercises.feedback: Like to wash describes a preferred routine, even though the speaker does not enjoy the chore.

exercises.prompt: We have a free afternoon tomorrow. I ___ the new exhibition with you.
exercises.feedback: Would love to see expresses a wish to do something on a specific occasion.

exercises.prompt: Would you mind ___ your voice a little? I am on a call.
exercises.feedback: Would you mind is followed by an -ing verb when making a polite request.

exercises.prompt: I am happy in my new flat. I ___ near the river. (like / live; current experience, use -ing)
acceptedAnswers: like living
exercises.feedback: An existing situation that the speaker enjoys is naturally expressed as like living.

exercises.prompt: To avoid losing data, I ___ my file after every major edit. (like / save; preferred routine, use a to-infinitive)
acceptedAnswers: like to save
exercises.feedback: Like to save expresses a regular choice or preferred habit.

exercises.prompt: Our friends arrive tonight. We ___ dinner with them. (would / like / have; specific wish, use to-infinitive)
acceptedAnswers: would like to have
exercises.feedback: Would like to have expresses a wish for the particular evening.

exercises.prompt: I missed the concert, and I still wish I had gone. I ___ it live. (would / love / see; use to have + past participle)
acceptedAnswers: would love to have seen
exercises.feedback: Would love to have seen expresses a missed chance to see something in the past.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I enjoy to cook for my friends.
acceptedAnswers: I enjoy cooking for my friends.
exercises.feedback: Enjoy is followed by cooking, not to cook.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I already live in this neighbourhood and I like to living here.
acceptedAnswers: I already live in this neighbourhood and I like living here.
exercises.feedback: For an existing experience, like living is appropriate; like to living is not grammatical.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Would you mind to turn the music down?
acceptedAnswers: Would you mind turning the music down?
exercises.feedback: Would you mind takes an -ing verb: turning.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I would love to have visit the exhibition last month.
acceptedAnswers: I would love to have visited the exhibition last month.
exercises.feedback: After to have, use the past participle visited to refer to a missed past opportunity.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one sentence using these words: I / enjoy / cook / for my family. Use the -ing form after enjoy.
acceptedAnswers: I enjoy cooking for my family.
speakingExercises.feedback: Enjoy + -ing expresses pleasure in an activity.

speakingExercises.prompt: Noah dislikes travelling to work on buses. Begin “Noah hates” and use the -ing form of commute followed by “by bus”.
acceptedAnswers: Noah hates commuting by bus.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hates commuting refers to a generally disliked repeated experience.

speakingExercises.prompt: You choose to check the windows before sleeping, although it is not enjoyable. Begin “I like” and use to + check followed by “the windows before bed”.
acceptedAnswers: I like to check the windows before bed.
speakingExercises.feedback: Like to check describes a chosen practice rather than pleasure in the task.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express one wish for today. Begin “I would like” or “I’d like” and finish with “to visit the new library today”.
acceptedAnswers: I would like to visit the new library today.
I'd like to visit the new library today.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would like to visit expresses a wish concerning a particular day.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a polite offer to a guest. Begin “Would you like” and end with “to sit by the window?”
acceptedAnswers: Would you like to sit by the window?
speakingExercises.feedback: Would you like + to-infinitive is a polite way to offer an option.

speakingExercises.prompt: Politely ask someone to wait one minute. Begin “Would you mind” and use waiting followed by “a minute?”
acceptedAnswers: Would you mind waiting a minute?
speakingExercises.feedback: Would you mind waiting follows the required -ing pattern.

speakingExercises.prompt: She missed a lecture and now wishes she had attended. Begin “She would love” and end with “the lecture”. Use “to have attended”.
acceptedAnswers: She would love to have attended the lecture.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would love to have attended expresses an unrealised past wish.

speakingExercises.prompt: Produce exactly two sentences. First, begin “I like” and say “walking in parks” as a general enjoyment. Second, begin “Today I would love” and say “to visit the botanical garden”.
acceptedAnswers: I like walking in parks. Today I would love to visit the botanical garden.
speakingExercises.feedback: Like walking states a general preference; would love to visit expresses today’s specific wish.

listeningExercises.audioText: I like cycling to work when the weather is nice. It helps me feel awake in the morning.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker generally enjoy?
choices: Cycling to work in good weather.
listeningExercises.feedback: Like cycling describes a generally enjoyable activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: I'd like to cycle to work tomorrow, but my bicycle is still at the repair shop.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker want to do tomorrow?
listeningExercises.feedback: I'd like to cycle is a specific wish about tomorrow.

listeningExercises.audioText: My brother enjoys running after work, even when the weather is cold.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the one-word activity immediately after “enjoys”.
acceptedAnswers: running
listeningExercises.feedback: Enjoys is followed by the -ing form running.

listeningExercises.audioText: I don't enjoy washing the car, but I like to do it early on Saturdays before the streets get busy.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why does the speaker mention an early Saturday routine?
choices: Washing the car is their favourite hobby.
They never wash the car at weekends.
They prefer to finish a disliked chore early.
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker dislikes the chore but prefers an early routine.

listeningExercises.audioText: Would you mind lowering the blinds? The afternoon sun is shining directly on my screen.
listeningExercises.prompt: What action is the listener being asked to take?
listeningExercises.feedback: Would you mind lowering is a polite request to lower the blinds.

listeningExercises.audioText: I would love to have visited the museum while we were there, but it was closed throughout our trip.
choices: Missing the chance to visit the museum.
Spending too much time inside the museum.
listeningExercises.feedback: Would love to have visited looks back on an opportunity that was not possible.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children would like to build a tree house during the holiday.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word infinitive phrase immediately after “would like”.
acceptedAnswers: to build
listeningExercises.feedback: Would like takes to build for a desired activity.

listeningExercises.audioText: I would prefer to have stayed longer, but my train left at six.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word perfect infinitive phrase immediately after “prefer”.
acceptedAnswers: to have stayed
listeningExercises.feedback: To have stayed indicates a preference for a different past outcome.
